items.title: Jehovah’s Day Will Come on Time
items.answer:
Have you ever waited for someone who was always late? Sooner or later you stop trusting their clock. Jehovah is not like that. His Word shows him to be a precise Timekeeper, and the book of Ezekiel proves it. 

Jehovah is a precise Timekeeper. In Ezekiel 7:3 we hear him declare: 'The end is now upon you.' That was not an idle threat. The prophet Ezekiel acted out Jehovah's judgment with signs: a brick under siege, rationed bread and measured water, and then 390 days lying on his left side and 40 days on his right side — each day representing a year. Those enacted years pointed to the exact year of Jerusalem's destruction, 607 B.C.E. Ezekiel could not have worked that timetable out himself; Jehovah gave it to him, and history proved it to the letter. Ezekiel had no doubt that Jehovah would prove to be an exact timekeeper, and he was not disappointed. When Jehovah set a time, he kept it — to the day.

When Jehovah's set time arrived, the Israelites had not changed their detestable ways, so he acted against them. Listen to how Ezekiel 7:4 puts it: 'My eye will not feel sorry for you; nor will I feel compassion, for I will bring upon you the results of your own ways, and you will suffer the consequences of your detestable deeds.' And verse 10 rings out: 'Look, the day! Look, it is coming!' Notice what that means. The people of Judah had warning after warning, prophet after prophet, year after year. But when the appointed day finally arrived, they were still the same — still idolatrous, still violent, still dismissive. So judgment came exactly on schedule. The delay was not slowness; it was mercy. The punctuality was not cruelty; it was justice keeping its word.

Knowing that Jehovah's day will come on time moves us to make wise use of our time. If the execution of his judgment against Jerusalem ran precisely on schedule, the same is true of the fulfillment we are living through now. That conviction produces urgency: the time still available for helping others to become God's servants is limited, so we carry out the disciple-making work with urgency. It also produces balance: we keep Jehovah's pure worship first and foremost in our life rather than chasing what this world counts as security. And it produces watchfulness: we do not squeeze our ministry into whatever time is left over at the end of the week.

One practical way we use our time wisely: we preach at the times when we are most likely to find people. Think about your territory. When are the people actually home? Early morning before work? Late afternoon? Sunday afternoons? Letters and phone messaging reach those who are never at their door. A wise publisher asks: 'When did I last find this householder at home?' and returns at that time. Small adjustments like that make our limited hours count for more.

So let us leave this Treasures part with three convictions firm in our hearts. First, Jehovah is a precise Timekeeper — his deadlines are trustworthy. Second, when his set time arrived, those who refused to change were swept away — so we take his warnings personally and change now. Third, because his day will come on time, we spend our days on what he counts as valuable: worship, family, and the preaching work, at the times people can actually be found. The end of this system is near — and Jehovah, our Timekeeper, will act right on time.

scriptures.quote: The end is now upon you, and I will unleash my anger against you, and I will judge you according to your ways and call you to account for all your detestable deeds.
scriptures.use: Jehovah announced the end in advance — the mark of a precise Timekeeper.

scriptures.quote: My eye will not feel sorry for you; nor will I feel compassion, for I will bring upon you the results of your own ways, and you will suffer the consequences of your detestable deeds. And you will have to know that I am Jehovah.
scriptures.use: When the set time arrived and Israel had not changed, he acted against them exactly as foretold.

scriptures.quote: Look, the day! Look, it is coming! Your turn has come; the rod has blossomed and presumptuousness has sprouted.
scriptures.use: The day Jehovah set did arrive — his timing is exact.

items.title: Spiritual Gems
items.answer:
Gem 1 — Eze 7:19 — In what sense will this prophecy be fulfilled? In the larger fulfillment, during the great tribulation, people will 'throw their silver into the streets' because they will finally realize that neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them in the day of Jehovah's fury. Materialism will be stripped of every promise it made. The lesson for us (w24.09 11 par. 14): strong faith that the end is imminent motivates us to reject materialism — live simply, resist unnecessary debt, do not become overly attached to possessions.

Other gems from this week's reading, Ezekiel 7-8:
1. From Eze 7:19: wealth becomes worthless exactly when you need rescue. That convicts me about overtime hours spent chasing things I do not need — I would rather have a simple life with time for the ministry than a full bank account that cannot save me.
2. From Eze 8:12: the elders committed their detestable acts 'in the darkness' while saying, 'Jehovah is not seeing us.' Self-deception is the most dangerous lie of all. This reminds me to keep my conscience clean even in things no colleague or family member will ever see — what I claim on my timesheets, what I watch when nobody knows.
3. From Eze 8:16: about 25 men stood with their backs to the temple, bowing to the sun. They had the appearance of worshippers in God's courtyard while facing in the opposite direction. I want to check my own direction, not just my appearance: does my conduct actually face Jehovah's way of worship, or do I merely stand near it?

scriptures.quote: They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will become abhorrent to them. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them in the day of Jehovah’s fury.
scriptures.use: In the larger fulfillment, riches will not save anyone during the great tribulation — the lesson is to reject materialism now.

scriptures.quote: He said to me: “Son of man, do you see what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each one in the inner rooms where his idols are displayed? For they are saying, ‘Jehovah is not seeing us. Jehovah has left the land.’”
scriptures.use: Hidden sin thrives on the self-deception that Jehovah does not see.

scriptures.quote: So he brought me to the inner courtyard of the house of Jehovah. There at the entrance of the temple of Jehovah, between the porch and the altar, were about 25 men with their backs to the temple of Jehovah and their faces to the east; they were bowing down to the sun in the east.
scriptures.use: A worshipper can stand in the right courtyard while facing in the wrong direction.

items.title: Bible Reading — Eze 8:7-18 (th study 2)
items.answer:
Context: In a vision Jehovah brings Ezekiel from Babylon to Jerusalem and digs past the surface — literally, through a hole in the wall. Inside the temple complex Ezekiel finds what the outsiders never saw: seventy elders burning incense to carved idols in a chamber of images (verses 7-13), women weeping over the idol Tammuz (verses 14-15), and about 25 men in the innermost courtyard with their backs to the temple, bowing to the sun (verses 16-18). Each time, Jehovah asks Ezekiel, 'Do you see?' — and each time the corruption is worse, ending with the warning in verse 18 that his fury will not be held back.

Lesson 1: Sin can hide inside what should be holy — the temple looked intact from the outside while idolatry worked in its inner rooms (Eze 8:12). Lesson 2: Courteous excuses do not cancel guilt — the men said 'Jehovah is not seeing us,' but the visions he sent proved the opposite. Lesson 3: Persistent, unrepented corruption finally exhausts Jehovah's patience (Eze 8:18).

Possible comment: "What strikes me in this reading is that the elders did their idolatry 'in the darkness' and said, 'Jehovah is not seeing us.' (Eze 8:12) It is a warning to me personally: nothing I do is really in the dark, and the safest heart is one that would not commit the act even if it could be hidden."

scriptures.quote: He said to me: “Son of man, do you see what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each one in the inner rooms where his idols are displayed? For they are saying, ‘Jehovah is not seeing us. Jehovah has left the land.’”
scriptures.use: The reading's key scene: hidden idolatry justified by the belief that Jehovah does not see.

items.title: Starting a Conversation — House to House (lmd lesson 1 point 4)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 1 point 4 — “Be observant. Ask yourself: ‘What is the person currently doing? What might he be thinking about?’ ‘What do the person’s clothing, appearance, or home tell me about his beliefs or culture?’ ‘Is this a good time to talk to the person?’”

HOUSE TO HOUSE — Daniel calls at a home in the late afternoon. Before speaking he observes: the person is watering her vegetable beds in the front garden, she is dressed for the evening market shift, and it is clearly a busy moment. He keeps the opening short, observes what she is doing, and starts with that.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good afternoon! Sorry to disturb you while you are watering — I couldn't help noticing your garden. Those pepper plants look really healthy."
Ruth (Householder): "Oh, thank you! I spend half my free time out here. My mother taught me to grow these."
Daniel (Publisher): "It shows. You can tell when someone really cares for a garden — everything is ordered, nothing is neglected. It's a nice peaceful spot, too. Is now a bad time? You look like you're on your way somewhere."
Ruth (Householder): "I'm heading to the market soon, actually. But I can talk for a minute."
Daniel (Publisher): "Then just one small thought while you water: this work you do with your hands — the daily care, the patience — the Bible says that kind of diligence is rewarded. And it raises a bigger question: who would you say is really in charge of whether our hard work finally pays off?"
Ruth (Householder): "Hm. Good question. I always say God decides the rain."
Daniel (Publisher): "Exactly — and the Bible's answer to that question is encouraging. Here, this brochure answers it directly; it's free. Read it while the sun is down and the watering is done — I promise it's short."
Ruth (Householder): "Okay, I'll take it. Thank you!"

Keys: Daniel carries out lmd lesson 1 point 4 — he observed what the person was doing (watering her garden), what her home told him (someone who values care and order), and whether it was a good time to talk (he checked, and kept it brief before her market shift). His opener grew out of his observation rather than out of a prepared script, which is exactly what the point trains us to do.

items.title: Following Up — House to House (lmd lesson 9 point 3)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 9 point 3 — “Listen carefully. Allow the person to express himself. Do not interrupt him or quickly dismiss his feelings, concerns, or objections. By paying attention, you show him that you care about what he thinks.”

HOUSE TO HOUSE, FOLLOWING UP — Daniel returns to the family that showed interest. Last time it was Ruth's son Kofi who showed interest; today Kofi is not home, so Daniel talks with Ruth, a family member other than the one who originally showed interest. He lets her express her concerns about her son and does not interrupt or dismiss them.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good afternoon, Ruth! Is Kofi home today?"
Ruth (Householder): "Ah, Daniel! No, Kofi has gone to his uncle's place. He will be back on Friday."
Daniel (Publisher): "Thank you. May I ask — how have you been finding all this? Kofi mentioned you had questions about what we teach."
Ruth (Householder): "Honestly? I have been thinking a lot. It is a big change, this religion you are teaching him. I grew up in my own church, and I am afraid that if he leaves it, his father will be furious. And me — who will bury me if something happens to me? These things matter."
Daniel (Publisher): "Those matters matter very much, and I am glad you told me. You are saying two things: this is a big change for the family, and the traditions matter to you — belonging, respect for your parents, even how you will be cared for at the end. Have I understood you?"
Ruth (Householder): "Yes. That is it exactly."
Daniel (Publisher): "Then may I share one thing? The Bible shows that honoring parents and caring for family is something Jehovah himself insists on — it is never at odds with true worship. And he promises that he will never abandon those who draw close to him. Perhaps Kofi can show you that in your own Bible on Friday — would you like to sit in with us for ten minutes then?"
Ruth (Householder): "Maybe I will listen in. Tell him to come early, before his father returns."

Keys: Daniel carries out lmd lesson 9 point 3 — he allowed Ruth to express herself fully, did not interrupt or quickly dismiss her feelings and objections, and repeated her concerns back to her so she knew he had paid attention. Only then did he share information that addressed what she actually said, and he used the follow-up visit to draw another family member into the truth.

items.title: Making Disciples — Help Your Student Prepare to Witness to a Relative (lmd lesson 12 point 3)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 12 point 3 — “Help your student set and reach goals. Use the ‘Goal’ feature in each lesson of Enjoy Life Forever! Help your student identify specific steps to reach both short-term and long-term goals. Commend your student regularly for his progress.”

MAKING DISCIPLES — Daniel helps his student prepare to witness to a relative: he turns the goal into small specific steps, uses the Goal feature of the Enjoy Life Forever! lesson, and commends the student for her progress.

Daniel (Publisher): "Ruth, you mentioned last week that your cousin Ama keeps asking why you no longer come to church with the family. Would you like to share your faith with her?"
Ruth (Householder): "I would love to — but I am scared, Daniel. What if she asks something I cannot answer?"
Daniel (Publisher): "That fear is normal, and it is exactly why we prepare together. Let us use the Goal feature in today's lesson. What is the goal, in one sentence?"
Ruth (Householder): "To give Ama a witness about why I changed — kindly, this weekend."
Daniel (Publisher): "Good. Now the steps. Step one: tonight, read the paragraph we studied and pick the one point that moved you most. Step two: Thursday, we prepare together — a simple opener, one scripture, and what you will do if you cannot answer a question. Step three: the weekend itself — you share it, and you tell me afterwards, whatever the result. Can you do that?"
Ruth (Householder): "I can. Honestly, breaking it into steps makes it feel possible."
Daniel (Publisher): "And Ruth — notice something before you go. Two months ago you were the one saying, 'I could never explain my faith.' Since then you have commented at the meeting twice and prepared a presentation. That is real progress, and Jehovah sees it. I am proud of you."
Ruth (Householder): "Thank you. With steps and a goal, I really think I can talk to Ama this weekend."

Keys: Daniel carries out lmd lesson 12 point 3 — he helped Ruth set a clear goal (a kind witness to her cousin), broke it into specific short-term steps with a date for each, kept the long-term goal of spiritual progress in view, and commended her sincerely for the progress she had already made.

items.title: Imagine the Outcome
items.answer:
Discussion. Open with the verse the conductor reads: Jehovah told unfaithful Israel, "I will bring upon you the results of your own ways, and you will suffer the consequences of your detestable deeds." (Eze 7:4) He is a precise Timekeeper, and the consequences of a course of action always arrive with it. The lesson: before embarking on any course, imagine the outcome — 'If only they were wise! They would ponder over this. They would think about their outcome.' (De 32:29)

ASK THE AUDIENCE (Read Proverbs 27:11 and Philippians 4:7): "What blessings do we enjoy from keeping our integrity?"
Sample comment: "The greatest blessing is one I cannot see but heaven can — my integrity makes Jehovah's heart rejoice. 'Be wise, my son, and make my heart rejoice, so that I can make a reply to him who taunts me.' (Pr 27:11) And right now, today, I get what no compromise can buy: 'the peace of God that surpasses all understanding' guarding my heart and my mental powers. (Php 4:7) A clean conscience that lets me sleep well at night is a blessing money cannot replicate."

ASK THE AUDIENCE (Read Psalm 38:3-8): "What bad consequences of giving in to sin might we imagine?"
Sample comment: "David describes the inside of a sinful course: 'My whole body is sick because of your indignation. There is no peace within my bones because of my sin,' and 'I have grown numb and become completely crushed; my anguished heart makes me groan aloud.' (Ps 38:3, 8) That is the outcome worth imagining before the temptation arrives: the guilt, the loss of peace, the shame before people we love — and worst of all, our own errors separating us from our God, so that he refuses to hear us. (Isa 59:2)"

PLAY THE VIDEO 'Imagine the Time' and ASK THE AUDIENCE: "What future blessings do you look forward to receiving in the new world?"
Sample comment: "When I imagine the time instead of the temptation, the pull of this world loses its grip. I look forward to welcoming back loved ones in the resurrection, to a body that finally obeys me instead of failing me, to work that satisfies, and above all to standing on the other side of Armageddon knowing I kept my integrity when it would have been so easy to give it away. Whatever this world offers me today, it cannot compete with that."

Conclusion: temptations are usually sold to us as small. So train the imagination now: picture yourself tomorrow morning after saying no — at peace, Jehovah's heart rejoicing, friendships intact; then picture the morning after compromise. The first picture is worth fighting for.

scriptures.quote: My eye will not feel sorry for you; nor will I feel compassion, for I will bring upon you the results of your own ways, and you will suffer the consequences of your detestable deeds.
scriptures.use: Jehovah lets the consequences of our chosen course arrive with it.

scriptures.quote: If only they were wise! They would ponder over this. They would think about their outcome.
scriptures.use: The command of the discussion: imagine the outcome before embarking on a course.

scriptures.quote: Be wise, my son, and make my heart rejoice, So that I can make a reply to him who taunts me.
scriptures.use: Integrity gives Jehovah something to answer the taunter with — a blessing worth imagining.

scriptures.quote: and the peace of God that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and your mental powers by means of Christ Jesus.
scriptures.use: The present blessing of a clean conscience.

scriptures.quote: My whole body is sick because of your indignation. There is no peace within my bones because of my sin.
scriptures.use: The imagined outcome of giving in to sin: loss of peace.

scriptures.quote: I have grown numb and become completely crushed; My anguished heart makes me groan aloud.
scriptures.use: Sin crushes from the inside long before anything else does.

scriptures.quote: No, your own errors have separated you from your God. Your sins have made him hide his face from you, And he refuses to hear you.
scriptures.use: The worst consequence to imagine: separation from Jehovah himself.

items.cite: Eze 7:4; De 32:29; Pr 27:11; Php 4:7; Ps 38:3-8; Isa 59:2; video “Imagine the Time”

items.title: Congregation Bible Study — Walk Courageously With God, Section 2 & chap. 22 (Jonathan)
items.answer: Study source: the book Walk Courageously With God! (wcg) — the Section 2 introduction 'From the Days of the Kings to the Rebuilding of Jerusalem' (wcg pp. 102-103), the Section 2 Timeline (wcg pp. 104-105), and chapter 22, 'His Loyalty Called for Courage' — the account of Jonathan (wcg chap. 22 pp. 106-109). The Bible account read: 1 Samuel 13:2, 19-23; 14:1-15; 16:21; 18:1-9; 19:4-6; 20:1-42; 23:16-18; 28:6-8; 31:1-6; 2 Samuel 1:17-27; 9:1-7. Below are prepared answers to every question across all three parts — the section introduction, the timeline, and the chapter's discussion, Dig Deeper, Reflect on the Lessons and Meditate on the Bigger Picture questions.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: Section 2 of the book opens — “From the Days of the Kings to the Rebuilding of Jerusalem” (wcg pp. 102-103). What will this section cover?
cbs.answer: This section spans some six centuries of Jehovah's people's history — from Jonathan, the son of King Saul, through David, the first truly faithful king, down to the return from exile in Babylon and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Along the way we meet Abigail, Nathan, Elijah, Daniel, Esther, and Nehemiah. Each faced real challenges: ruling over Jehovah's rebellious people, coping with rulers who went astray, and standing up for the truth while the nation drifted into apostasy and wickedness. The courage of men and women under exactly those pressures is what we need to imitate today.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: Looking at the Section 2 Timeline (wcg pp. 104-105), what pattern do the dates and world powers reveal?
cbs.answer: The timeline moves through four periods — United Kingdom, Divided Kingdom, Exile to Babylon, and the Postexilic period. Beside the people, the world powers march in sequence: Egypt, then Assyria (after 874 B.C.E.), Babylon from 625 B.C.E., and Medo-Persia from 539 B.C.E. Fixed dates anchor the account: Solomon's temple completed 1027 B.C.E., the kingdom divided 997 B.C.E., Jerusalem destroyed 607 B.C.E., the Jews released from Babylon 537 B.C.E., the temple rebuilt 515 B.C.E., and Jerusalem's walls completed 455 B.C.E. Jehovah ruled both his people and the nations on schedule — a powerful boost to our trust in his timing as we approach his day.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: In what ways did Jonathan show courage?
cbs.answer: First in battle: Jonathan and his armor-bearer — two armed men — attacked an entire Philistine garrison, convinced that nothing can hinder Jehovah from saving by many or by few (1 Sam 14:6). Then in circumstances that cost far more: his father Saul turned bad, turning disobedient to Jehovah, yet Jonathan put his loyalty to God first. As a man likely nearing 50 he befriended young David, showed not a trace of jealousy, gave David his own fighting gear, stood up for David when his own father hurled a spear at him, and warned David of Saul's murderous plans even though Saul was still a mighty warrior. Courage on the battlefield — and courage at home.

scriptures.quote: Perhaps Jehovah will act in our behalf, for nothing can hinder Jehovah from saving by many or by few.
scriptures.use: The conviction that carried Jonathan up the rocky pass — and through every family conflict that followed.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 1
cbs.answer: They were a seafaring people from the Aegean region who settled on the coastal plain of Canaan, organized in five city-states — Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron. They were Israel's persistent enemies, militarily ahead with iron weapons and war chariots, and they kept the Israelites disarmed by forbidding Hebrew blacksmiths. In this account a Philistine garrison had moved into Michmash and was plundering the land unchecked — the menace that Jonathan and his armor-bearer, two men with two swords, walked toward that morning.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 2
cbs.q: How does the word “pim” testify to the accuracy of this account? (w05 3/15 29) [Picture A: a pim weight stone]
cbs.answer: First Samuel 13:21 mentions a weight called a "pim" — a term later translators did not understand, some even turning it into a place name. Archaeology settled it: small stone weights stamped with a sign reading "pim" have been excavated in Palestine, each weighing about two thirds of a shekel — the very price the Philistine blacksmiths charged for sharpening tools. A writer living centuries later could not have known that word. Samuel used the precise commercial vocabulary of his own day, which is exactly what you would expect from an authentic contemporary account.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 3
cbs.q: What might have made it difficult to cross the ravine pass of Michmash? What may have helped Jonathan to do so? (it “Michmash” par. 4) [Picture B: possible location of the ravine pass of Michmash]
cbs.answer: Michmash sat on a ridge flanked by steep ravines; the pass between the cliffs was a narrow, rocky defile — difficult even for a column of soldiers, and seemingly impossible for two unarmed men climbing up toward a fortified garrison. Picture B shows how forbidding the terrain is. What helped Jonathan? His settled conviction that numbers mean nothing to Jehovah — "nothing can hinder Jehovah from saving by many or by few" — and the faith of his armor-bearer, who told him to go ahead, saying that he was with him heart and soul. Faith for the climb, plus one loyal companion.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 4
cbs.q: To what extent did David go to keep his promise to care for Jonathan's family? (it “Mephibosheth” No. 2 par. 1)
cbs.answer: All the way. Years after Jonathan fell at Gilboa, David — now secure on the throne — asked whether anyone remained of Saul's house to whom he could exercise loyal love for Jonathan's sake. He found Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, crippled in both feet, summoned him to Jerusalem, restored Saul's fields to him, and had him eat at the king's table regularly, treating him like one of the king's own sons. David honored a vow made decades earlier, when keeping it brought him no political benefit whatsoever. That is what loyalty between true friends looks like when it is tested by time.

cbs.label: Reflect · A
cbs.q: Jonathan put his loyalty to Jehovah ahead of his loyalty to Saul. In what situations might we face a similar conflict of loyalties?
cbs.answer: Whenever someone we love walks against Jehovah's standards: a parent forbidding meetings or service, a marriage mate opposing the truth, a close relative pressing us into a dishonest business deal, family pressure to celebrate unscriptural holidays or share in political activity, or relatives urging us to marry someone who does not serve Jehovah. Jonathan shows the pattern: he never stopped loving or respecting his father, but where Saul's course crossed Jehovah's will, Jonathan sided with God — even when it cost him a spear thrown by his own father.

cbs.label: Reflect · B
cbs.q: What does Jonathan's relationship with David teach you about friendship?
cbs.answer: That real friendship takes initiative and gives generously. Jonathan — the older, the crown prince — initiated the friendship, sealed it with a vow, and gave David his own fighting gear including his bow, though he was himself a renowned archer. He defended his friend at real personal cost, kept his promises for decades, and even entrusted his family's future to David. And notice the finest gift of all: when David was at his lowest, hiding at Horesh, Jonathan went to him and helped him find strength in Jehovah. Friendship that only takes is common; friendship that strengthens faith is worth seeking and worth becoming.

scriptures.quote: Jonathan the son of Saul now went out to David at Horesh, and he helped him find strength in Jehovah.
scriptures.use: The highest work of a friend: strengthening the friend's grip on Jehovah.

cbs.label: Reflect · C
cbs.q: What does Jonathan's relationship with David teach you about humility?
cbs.answer: Jonathan had every human reason to feel entitled: he was the heir, some 30 years older than David, a proven warrior. Then Jehovah chose David to be the next king instead of him. Rather than sulking or scheming, Jonathan accepted God's choice and told David plainly: 'You will be king over Israel, and I will become second to you' — and he meant it. Humility allowed him to rejoice in another man's blessing instead of resenting it. When Jehovah's arrangement gives someone else the honor we quietly thought was ours, our peace, our friendships, and our usefulness all depend on that same humility.

scriptures.quote: Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will not find you; you will be king over Israel, and I will become second to you;
scriptures.use: Jonathan's humility stated out loud: content to be second in Jehovah's arrangement.

cbs.label: Reflect · D
cbs.q: What does Jonathan's relationship with David teach you about loyalty?
cbs.answer: That loyalty is proved under pressure, not in comfortable times. Saul's love for David withered into bitter jealousy, yet Jonathan's vow never wavered; he risked the spear, warned David of his father's intentions, and kept the friendship to the end. His loyalty ran in both directions: he stayed loyally at his undeserving father's side in battle until both fell at Gilboa. And David repaid it — grieving, 'I am distressed over you, my brother Jonathan; you were very dear to me,' and years later searching out Mephibosheth to care for him. Loyalty like that outlives the grave.

scriptures.quote: I am distressed over you, my brother Jonathan; You were very dear to me.
scriptures.use: David's dirge — proof that Jonathan's loyalty was felt long after his death.

cbs.label: Reflect · E
cbs.q: In what other ways might you imitate the courage of Jonathan?
cbs.answer: In the everyday forms courage takes: defending a Bible truth or the neutral stand at school or work when it will cost something; speaking up kindly when a fellow believer is being treated unfairly; giving a friend honest counsel even when it risks the friendship; refusing dishonest gain even though the family's income seems to depend on it; and daring to reach out to someone who is isolated or discouraged. Jonathan climbed a rocky ravine to reach his friend — courage often just means going where loyalty points, despite the fear in your own chest.

cbs.label: Meditate · A
cbs.q: What does this account teach me about Jehovah?
cbs.answer: That he is a God who saves 'by many or by few' — the size of the enemy and the difficulty of the terrain mean nothing when his servants act in faith. He notices loyalty even when it is tested by one's own family, and he rewards it. He ties victory to obedience rather than to weapons. And he treasures friendship between his servants so highly that he preserved the record of Jonathan and David's vow for our instruction — and kept David's promise alive through Mephibosheth long after both men had died.

scriptures.quote: for nothing can hinder Jehovah from saving by many or by few.
scriptures.use: The principle the whole account demonstrates about Jehovah.

cbs.label: Meditate · B
cbs.q: How does the account tie in with Jehovah's purposes?
cbs.answer: Jehovah had chosen David to be Israel's next king — the forefather of the promised Messiah. Jonathan's loyalty helped protect that chosen line through years when Saul's jealousy would otherwise have crushed it: his warning and his friendship kept David alive. The account also previews greater things. The Greater David, Jesus Christ, has a loyal friend class who stick with him in his trials, and Jonathan's willing spirit — content to be second so that God's purpose advanced — mirrors the attitude Christ's followers cultivate today as they support the Kingdom rather than seek personal prominence.

cbs.label: Meditate · C
cbs.q: What would I like to ask Jonathan in the resurrection?
cbs.answer: I would love to sit with him on that rocky ridge above Michmash and ask: 'When you looked down at the garrison — just the two of you — what went through your mind?' I would ask how he kept bitterness out of his heart when Jehovah chose David over him, and what it cost to love both his father and his friend when the two became enemies. And I would thank him for proving, at the cost of his own throne, that putting loyalty to Jehovah first is the safest course a man can ever take.

scriptures.quote: Perhaps Jehovah will act in our behalf, for nothing can hinder Jehovah from saving by many or by few.
scriptures.use: The verse at the heart of the chapter's account of Jonathan's courage.

items.cite: wcg pp. 102-109 (section 2 intro, timeline, chap. 22) · 1 Samuel; 2 Samuel 1; 9

items.comment: Honest answer — many of us grew up with the world's idea of friendship. Social media turns friendship into a numbers game: followers, likes, group chats. Some young people look only to their peers for advice and comfort, and others decide they do not need anyone at all, that they are better off alone. But those views come from the spirit of this world. As Witnesses taking our stand for pure worship, we let Jehovah reshape how we see friendship.
items.insight: The article opens with a diagnostic question because how you define friendship quietly decides whose voice you will listen to when the real tests come.
items.apply: Ask yourself this week whose voice carries most weight with you — peers' or mature ones who serve Jehovah — and deliberately sit with one mature friend at the meeting.

paraNotes.points: The world reduces friendship to quantity — many friends, only peers for advice and comfort — or claims we need no friends at all; taking our stand includes refusing to let the world's spirit shape our view of friendship.

items.q: (a) How did Jesus show that he valued meaningful friendships? (b) According to Ecclesiastes 4:9-12, what can good friendships provide?
items.comment: Jesus chose friends and said so. On the last night of his life he told his apostles: "You are the ones who have stuck with me in my trials." (Luke 22:28; John 15:15) Notice — he valued them even while knowing one would betray him. And Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 shows what true friends give: strength and comfort in distress, and real protection — "someone may overpower one alone, but two together can take a stand against him." Friendship with the right people is spiritual armor, not decoration.

scriptures.quote: However, you are the ones who have stuck with me in my trials;
scriptures.use: Jesus commended his faithful apostles as friends at the hardest moment of his life.

scriptures.quote: And someone may overpower one alone, but two together can take a stand against him.
scriptures.use: The verse the article is built on — friends make the stand for pure worship possible.

scriptures.quote: A true friend shows love at all times And is a brother who is born for times of distress.
scriptures.use: The test of friendship is not the smooth season but the distress.

items.insight: Jesus was never too busy, too important, or too near death to invest in friends — the friendships he built carried meaning even on his final night.
items.apply: Message or call a friend this week who is quietly going through a trial — not to fix anything, just to stick with them the way the apostles stuck with Jesus.

paraNotes.points: Jesus viewed his faithful apostles as friends who 'stuck with me in my trials'; a true friend sticks close in 'times of distress' (Prov 17:17); Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 shows true friends strengthen, comfort, and help us take a stand.
paraNotes.highlight: Footnote: although verses 9-12 are often applied to marriage, the passage is primarily about the value of friendship — so friendship deserves deliberate cultivation, not leftover time.

items.q: What will we consider in this article?
items.comment: The article takes us into Daniel's life. We will see how true friends helped a young man make the choice to serve Jehovah, how they helped him when temptation came and when a seemingly impossible challenge faced him, and how his best Friend — Jehovah himself — supported him even when he stood completely alone. We will also see how parents and other mature ones can help fill a young person's need for friends today.
items.insight: The roadmap is Daniel's life in four settings — choice, temptation, impossible challenge, isolation — which happen to be the four places every young person needs a friend.
items.apply: Read the article with the young people in your family or study group in mind, and plan one friendship-building arrangement for this week.

paraNotes.points: Preview: true friends help a young person serve Jehovah faithfully; parents and mature ones can fill that need; Daniel's example shows friendship's help under choice, temptation, seemingly impossible challenges, and isolation — with Jehovah as his best Friend.

items.q: What challenges did young Daniel face?
items.comment: Imagine being Daniel: probably just a teenager when Nebuchadnezzar made Judah subject to Babylon, then taken into exile and brought hundreds of kilometers away to Babylon for training — far from home, separated from his family, surrounded by a foreign language, religion, and court. Many young ones today face something similar: a move, boarding school, university, a new job far from the congregation. Distance from supportive friends is a real challenge, and Daniel's story shows it can be met.

scriptures.quote: In time Jehovah gave King Jehoiakim of Judah into his hand,
scriptures.use: The opening of Daniel's trial: Judah's unfaithfulness brought Babylonian subjection.

items.insight: Daniel's trial began with geography — the loss of home and family. Isolation is a test of loyalty, not a sign that Jehovah has forgotten you.
items.apply: If someone from your congregation recently moved away or left for school, be their friend at a distance — a call or voice note this week.

paraNotes.points: Daniel, probably a teenager, saw Judah lose Jehovah's favor and made subject to Babylon (620 B.C.E.); a few years later he was taken into exile to Babylon for training — far from home and family (Dan 1:2, 3-6).

items.q: Who may have helped Daniel make the choice to serve Jehovah?
items.comment: Someone had to teach Daniel God's laws — he had already "resolved in his heart" before Babylon. His parents likely led the way; even his name, "My Judge Is God," may have expressed their desire. And think of Jeremiah: appointed in 647 B.C.E., before Daniel was born, preaching to prominent men who may well have included Daniel's family — and Daniel later studied Jeremiah's prophecies for himself. So Daniel likely had parents plus a bold prophet shaping his heart while he was young.

scriptures.quote: These words that I am commanding you today must be on your heart, … and you must inculcate them in your sons and speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk on the road and when you lie down and when you get up.
scriptures.use: How parents like Daniel's would have prepared a child's heart — constant, natural spiritual conversation.

items.insight: Loyalty to Jehovah is usually grown into a young person before the test arrives — by parents who talk about God naturally and by faithful examples he can watch.
items.apply: Parents: put one natural spiritual conversation with each child on this week's calendar — in the car, at the table, on a walk — De 6:7 style.

paraNotes.points: Daniel had 'resolved in his heart' to follow God's laws before exile (Dan 1:8) — someone taught him; his parents may have expressed their desire in his very name, 'My Judge Is God' (De 6:6, 7).

Jeremiah, appointed in 647 B.C.E. before Daniel's birth, delivered Jehovah's messages to prominent men who may have included Daniel's family; Daniel later consulted Jeremiah's prophecies (Jer 25:11; 29:10; Dan 9:1, 2) — in Jeremiah he may have seen a bold, determined example of faith.

items.q: How can parents and other mature Christians help young ones today to remain loyal to Jehovah?
items.comment: By the same pattern. Parents, take the article's questions personally: Are my children prepared for tests of neutrality? How will they respond to temptations at school and online? Are they ready to take their stand during the great tribulation? Then act: discuss spiritual topics regularly, teach them to participate at meetings, work with them in the ministry. And young people especially benefit from time with mature friends — examples of faith and loyalty like Jeremiah.
items.insight: The best protection is preparation: the question is not when the tests come but whether the help is already in place before they do.
items.apply: Choose one child or young person in the congregation to encourage this month — offer to study with them or take them in the ministry.

paraNotes.points: Daniel's parents, Jeremiah, or other faithful servants of Jehovah were likely a good influence on him and helped him develop a close personal relationship with God.

Parents today should ask whether their children are ready for tests of neutrality, temptations at school and online, and the great tribulation — then deepen the children's love for Jehovah by regular spiritual discussion, meeting participation, working in the ministry, and time with examples of faith and loyalty.

items.q: What dangerous situation did Daniel and other young Hebrews find themselves in?
items.comment: Captivity brought temptations they had never faced at home. Immediately, the Babylonians tried to force them to adapt to their ways and customs, and the training for the king's palace would keep exposing them to situations that tested their loyalty to Jehovah. It is a warning for any young Christian entering a new environment — school, workplace, university: new freedom always comes packaged with new tests.
items.insight: The danger did not come with a warning label — it arrived disguised as opportunity: education, career, palace service.
items.apply: If you or your child is entering a new environment this term, decide before you arrive what you will never do — like Daniel did.

paraNotes.points: In captivity the young Hebrews faced temptations unknown at home: forced adaptation to Babylonian ways and customs, and palace training that would continually expose them to tests of loyalty.

items.q: What was the first test of loyalty that the young Jews faced?
items.comment: Food from the king's table — including things the Mosaic Law called unclean (Dan 1:5, 8). It looked minor, and they had every excuse: they were captives who were not free to do what they wanted, and it would not be wise to anger the king. But notice how big tests usually begin — in something that seems small. Daniel's answer was made easy because he had resolved in his heart in advance what he would not do.

scriptures.quote: But Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies or with the wine he drank. So he asked the principal court official for permission not to defile himself in this way.
scriptures.use: The decision was settled in advance — that is why the test found no vacillation.

items.insight: The first test rarely looks like the big one — it looks manageable, excusable. Integrity is decided in 'what is least.'
items.apply: Name one 'small' compromise you have been excusing — king's-delicacies size — and settle it this week.

paraNotes.points: First test: the king's order to eat food from the royal table, including food unclean under the Mosaic Law (Dan 1:5, 8) — it seemed minor, and the captives could have excused themselves out of fear of the king.

items.q: How did Daniel's choice of friends prove wise? (See also picture.)
items.comment: Notice who stayed loyal: of all the Hebrew youths selected for training, only four are mentioned — Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Those four helped one another resist the temptation and stayed faithful together, and Jehovah blessed them. The picture makes the point visually: they did not each fight alone; they stood as one. In a hostile place, even one loyal friend can be the difference between standing and falling.

scriptures.quote: And the true God gave these four youths knowledge and insight into every kind of writing and wisdom; and Daniel was given understanding in all sorts of visions and dreams.
scriptures.use: The blessing that followed their united stand: Jehovah honored all four.

items.insight: Friendship here was never just companionship — it was mutual resistance: they made loyalty easier for one another.
items.apply: Identify the friend who strengthens your loyalty, and put something spiritual together with them on this week's schedule.

paraNotes.points: Only four of the selected Hebrews are mentioned as staying loyal — Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; they helped one another resist temptation, refused the king's food together, and Jehovah blessed them (Dan 1:6-12, 17).
paraNotes.highlight: The picture of Daniel and his three friends standing together visualizes the point: they resisted as one, not as four individuals.

items.q: What can help young ones today to fight temptations successfully?
items.comment: Two things. First, choose companions who are determined to remain loyal to Jehovah and to resist the pull of the world (1 John 2:15-17). Second, be faithful in "what is least" — the small compromises — because faithfulness there prepares you for the bigger tests that come later (Luke 16:10). So ask yourself honestly: who are my closest friends, and would they refuse the king's delicacies with me — or talk me into them?

scriptures.quote: The person faithful in what is least is faithful also in much, and the person unrighteous in what is least is unrighteous also in much.
scriptures.use: The little compromises are the training ground for the big tests.

items.insight: Temptation is usually social before it is personal — your circle sets your defaults.
items.apply: Audit your circle this week: distance yourself from one pull toward the world, and invest an hour in a friend who builds you up.

paraNotes.points: Choose companions determined to remain loyal to Jehovah and resist the pull of the world (1 John 2:15-17); faithfulness in 'what is least' (Luke 16:10) brings Jehovah's blessing and support and builds faithfulness for bigger tests later in life.

items.q: What seemingly impossible challenge did Daniel and his friends face?
items.comment: Nebuchadnezzar demanded the impossible: his advisers had to tell him what he had dreamed and then interpret it — something no human could do — or be put to death. Daniel and his friends were numbered among the wise men, so they faced execution for a failure they could not even prevent. And notice the article's observation: throughout this trial, Daniel and his three friends stood together. Impossible challenges were never meant to be carried solo.

scriptures.quote: If you do not make the dream known to me, there is only one penalty for all of you.
scriptures.use: The king's impossible demand: reveal the dream or die.

items.insight: An impossible demand becomes a shared burden when friends stand together — panic isolates, friendship stabilizes.
items.apply: Whatever feels impossible in your life right now, tell one trusted friend about it this week instead of carrying it silently.

paraNotes.points: Nebuchadnezzar insisted his advisers both relate and interpret his dream — impossible for any human (Dan 2:3, 9-11) — on pain of death; Daniel and his friends were among the wise men in danger of execution, and they stood together throughout the trial.

items.q: How did the young Hebrews support one another? (See also pictures.)
items.comment: Daniel bought time by approaching the king tactfully, and then he went straight to his friends — not to borrow their wisdom, but to borrow their prayers: "He asked them to pray for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this secret." (Dan 2:18) Their heartfelt prayers were answered, the secret was revealed to Daniel, and all four were spared and given positions of honor. They could not interpret the dream either — but they could pray together, and that made all the difference.

scriptures.quote: He asked them to pray for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this secret, so that Daniel and his companions would not be destroyed along with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
scriptures.use: Support among true friends took the form of asking others to pray for him.

items.insight: Facing the impossible, Daniel used his friends' faith as well as his own — asking others to pray for you is humility, not weakness.
items.apply: This week, ask one mature friend to pray for a specific matter you are facing — and offer to pray for theirs.

paraNotes.points: Daniel approached the king tactfully for time, then asked his friends to pray for mercy concerning the secret (Dan 2:18); Jehovah revealed the dream and its interpretation, sparing them all and giving them positions of honor (Dan 2:19, 47-49).
paraNotes.highlight: The picture shows the four young men praying together — their support was mutual prayer, not just mutual encouragement.

items.q: What lessons can we learn from this account? (Galatians 6:2)
items.comment: Three lessons. First, you do not need to face trials alone — never let pride or embarrassment stop you from seeking help. Second, do not hesitate to ask others to pray about a matter for you (2 Cor 1:11). Third, remember who you are actually asking: the "Hearer of prayer" can do far beyond what we ask (Ps 65:2; Eph 3:20). And Galatians 6:2 shows it goes both ways — we carry one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of the Christ.

scriptures.quote: Go on carrying the burdens of one another, and in this way you will fulfill the law of the Christ.
scriptures.use: The other half of the lesson: we are the friends who carry, not only the ones who ask.

scriptures.quote: O Hearer of prayer, to you people of all sorts will come.
scriptures.use: The One being asked in Daniel 2:18 — prayer really has a Hearer.

items.insight: The account reverses our instinct: strength in trial flows through admitted need and shared prayer, not through quiet independence.
items.apply: Start a small prayer-circle habit: two friends, one specific matter, one check-in this week.

paraNotes.points: Lessons: never face trials alone — do not let pride or embarrassment prevent seeking help; ask others to pray about a matter for you (2 Cor 1:11); rely on the 'Hearer of prayer' who can do more than we ask (Ps 65:2; Eph 3:20); friends who serve Jehovah supply strength to endure (Gal 6:2).

items.q: What trial did Daniel face in his old age?
items.comment: Even in his 90's, serving under King Darius after Babylon fell, Daniel was envied and plotted against. Enemies manipulated the king into banning prayer to anyone but the king for thirty days — and Daniel, refusing to comply, was thrown into the lions' pit. There he appeared to be alone in the most literal sense: no human friend, no congregation, just an old man among lions. The article's question deserves our pause: but was he truly alone?
items.insight: Old age and long faithfulness do not exempt anyone from trials — but decades of friendship with Jehovah pay their dividend exactly there.
items.apply: Never let a trial make you feel abandoned: memorize one 'Jehovah is with you' scripture this week to carry into isolated moments.

paraNotes.points: In his 90's under Darius, envious officials plotted Daniel's death and manipulated the king into a law forbidding prayer to any god but the king; Daniel's refusal sent him to the lions' pit — apparently alone, without human friends (Dan 6:4-16).

items.q: According to Daniel 6:19-23, how did having a strong friendship with Jehovah help Daniel?
items.comment: Jehovah rescued him miraculously — he sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths. And Daniel's own explanation afterward is beautiful: "My God sent his angel and shut the mouth of the lions, … for I was found innocent before him." (Dan 6:22) His friendship with Jehovah was not a feeling; it was innocence maintained before God over a lifetime, and it held when his life hung in the balance. His best Friend carried him through the night with the lions.

scriptures.quote: My God sent his angel and shut the mouth of the lions, and they have not harmed me, for I was found innocent before him; nor have I done any wrong to you, O king.
scriptures.use: The rescue Daniel credited to his best Friend — and to the innocence his friendship had maintained.

items.insight: Daniel's rescue was tied to being 'found innocent before him' — friendship with God rests on a clean standing maintained daily, then trusted in crisis.
items.apply: Keep your conscience clean this week on one specific point — the friendship you will lean on later is being built right now.

paraNotes.points: Daniel 6:19-23 records the miraculous rescue: Jehovah's angel shut the mouths of the lions; Daniel's testimony credited his God and his innocence before him (Dan 6:22) — his unwavering faith in his best Friend sustained him when his life hung in the balance.

items.q: Why is drawing close to Jehovah important, and how can we do this? (See also pictures and the box “Jehovah—Our Father, Our God and Friend.”)
items.comment: Because isolation can happen to any of us — a remote assignment, an unexpected move, limited health, even imprisonment. In those moments God's friends are never truly alone: "Where can I escape from your spirit, and where can I run away from your face?" (Ps 139:7-10) The box gives practical steps: communicate with Jehovah in prayer; spend time listening to him through Bible reading and study, learning who he is; and be patient — building trust and a relationship takes time, and Jehovah wants that relationship with you.

scriptures.quote: Where can I escape from your spirit, And where can I run away from your face?
scriptures.use: Nowhere — which is why the isolated servant is never truly alone.

scriptures.quote: Even there your hand would lead me And your right hand would take hold of me.
scriptures.use: The promise that reaches the lions' pit, the remote assignment, and the hospital room alike.

items.insight: The lions' pit principle scales down to every lonely room: the same Jehovah who shut the lions' mouths walks in there with you — closeness with him is the one friendship no distance can break.
items.apply: Pick one of the box's three areas — communicate, spend time together, be patient — and practice it daily this week.

paraNotes.points: Isolation can come through a remote assignment, an unexpected move, limited health, or imprisonment; God's friends are never truly alone — Jehovah offers protection and care wherever we are (Ps 139:7-10).
paraNotes.highlight: The box 'Jehovah—Our Father, Our God and Friend' gives three practical steps for those struggling to trust him: communicate in prayer, spend time together in Bible reading and study, and be patient — building trust takes time, and Jehovah wants a relationship with you.

items.q: Why do we need to strengthen our friendships now? (1 Thessalonians 5:2, 11)
items.comment: Because "Jehovah's day" is approaching — and it will come "exactly as a thief in the night." Paul's counsel fits our times perfectly: keep encouraging one another and building one another up. Peter felt the same urgency: knowing "the end of all things has drawn close," he wrote, "Above all things, have intense love for one another." Friendships built now, before the pressure peaks, are what will hold us together when it does.

scriptures.quote: For you yourselves know very well that Jehovah’s day is coming exactly as a thief in the night.
scriptures.use: Why friendships must be built now: the day arrives without warning.

scriptures.quote: Therefore, keep encouraging one another and building one another up, just as you are in fact doing.
scriptures.use: What true friends are for as the day approaches.

scriptures.quote: Above all things, have intense love for one another, because love covers a multitude of sins.
scriptures.use: Peter's matching counsel: intense love among friends, 'above all things.'

items.insight: Friendship is not a nice-to-have for the end times; it is infrastructure — love among friends is what holds a congregation together under pressure.
items.apply: Build one friendship deliberately this month: a standing arrangement — coffee after the meeting, a weekly call, family worship together.

paraNotes.points: True friends help us make wise decisions as we approach 'Jehovah's day,' which comes like a thief (1 Thess 5:2); they encourage and build us up (1 Thess 5:11); knowing 'the end of all things has drawn close,' Peter urged intense love for one another (1 Pet 4:7, 8).

items.q: What should we look for in true friends, and what will be the outcome if we choose them wisely?
items.comment: Look for friends who inspire and guide you — congregation members who, like Jeremiah, are examples of faith and loyalty. Surround yourself with those who strengthen your resolve to stay loyal to Jehovah. Humbly ask others to pray for you when needed. And above all, never forget who your best Friend is: "I will never leave you, and I will never abandon you." (Heb 13:5) With Jehovah's help, together we can take our stand — and enjoy friendships that last forever.

scriptures.quote: I will never leave you, and I will never abandon you.
scriptures.use: The promise of the best Friend of all — the anchor under every other friendship.

items.insight: The article ends where it began — with the stand we must take — but its final word is not our effort; it is the Friend who never leaves.
items.apply: Write down three friends who help you take your stand — and thank one of them personally this week.

paraNotes.points: Seek out congregation members who inspire and guide like Jeremiah, surround yourself with those who strengthen your resolve, humbly ask others to pray for you, and above all remember Jehovah, your best Friend, who will never abandon you (Heb 13:5) — with him, together we can take our stand and enjoy friendships that last forever.

recap.q: How can true friends help us when we face temptation?
recap.comment: Daniel and his three friends refused the king's food together and were blessed for it. Choose companions determined to remain loyal to Jehovah, be faithful in 'what is least,' and let true friends help you resist the pull of the world — faithfulness in the little things prepares you for the bigger tests later.

recap.q: How can true friends help us when we struggle with seemingly impossible challenges?
recap.comment: When Nebuchadnezzar's impossible demand threatened their lives, Daniel approached the king for time and then asked his friends to pray for mercy concerning the secret. Jehovah answered, revealed the dream, and spared them all. Never let pride or embarrassment prevent you from seeking help; ask others to pray for you and rely on the 'Hearer of prayer.'

recap.q: How can true friends help us when we are isolated?
recap.comment: In the lions' pit Daniel seemed to have no human friend — yet his best Friend, Jehovah, sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths. Whether through an assignment, a move, poor health, or imprisonment, God's friends are never truly alone; drawing close to Jehovah daily means his support and care reach you wherever you are.

daily.scripture: I was especially fond of the sons of men.
daily.comment: The ransom teaches us that Jesus cares deeply for people, especially for his disciples. ( John 13:1 ) For example, Jesus knew that some aspects of his earthly ministry would be very challenging, in particular his painful death. Yet, in carrying out his assignment on earth, he did not simply go through the motions. Instead, Jesus put his whole heart into preaching, teaching, and ministering to others. Even on the day of his death, Jesus took time to wash the feet of his apostles and give them many parting words of comfort and instruction. ( John 13:12-15 ) Then while he was on the stake, Jesus took a few moments to give hope to a dying criminal and to arrange for his own mother’s care. ( Luke 23:42, 43; John 19:26, 27 ) Thus Jesus’ deep love was expressed not only through his death but also through his entire life course on earth. w25.01 23 ¶11 December 21-27

daily.scripture: He bore the punishment for our peace, and because of his wounds we were healed.
daily.comment: The Bible uses a word picture to help us understand the freedom that comes from true forgiveness. Because of our sinful nature and inclination, we are likened to “slaves of sin.” But thanks to Jehovah’s forgiveness, we are like slaves who have been “set free from sin.” ( Rom. 6:17, 18; Rev. 1:5 ) Yes, Jehovah’s forgiveness gives us the exhilarating feeling of being set free from slavery. Because of the ransom sacrifice that Jehovah provided through his Son, we are figuratively spoken of as being healed. ( 1 Pet. 2:24 ) The ransom makes possible the full repair of our relationship with Jehovah, which has been damaged by spiritual sickness. Just as a person who has been healed of a serious illness feels intense joy, we too rejoice when we are healed spiritually and regain Jehovah’s favor as a result of his forgiveness. w25.02 11 ¶16; 13 ¶17 December 21-27

daily.scripture: If you keep on doing these things, you will by no means ever fail.
daily.comment: In the parable of the talents, Jesus spoke of two slaves who were faithful to their master and one who was not. ( Matt. 25:14-30 ) The two faithful slaves represent faithful anointed Christians. The Master, Jesus, invites them to “enter into the joy of [their] master.” They receive their heavenly reward, the first resurrection. ( Matt. 25:21, 23; Rev. 20:5b ) On the other hand, the bad example of the sluggish slave provides a warning for anointed ones. How so? They must prove to be industrious and diligent. In the parable of the talents, as in the parable of the virgins, Jesus was not predicting that the anointed would become sluggish. Rather, he was explaining what would happen if ever they did lose their zeal. They would fail to make their “calling and choosing sure for [themselves],” and they would not be permitted to enter into the heavenly Kingdom. w24.09 22 ¶10; 23 ¶12-13 December 21-27

daily.scripture: Make sure of the more important things.
daily.comment: All of us want to be able to provide for our own needs and for those of our family. ( Eccl. 7:12; 1 Tim. 5:8 ) When deciding whether to accept a job, we understandably will consider how much money we will earn. However, a person might be walking primarily by sight if that is the only factor he takes into account. If we are walking by faith, we will also consider how the job could affect our friendship with Jehovah. We could ask ourselves: ‘Would the job require me to engage in practices that Jehovah hates?’ ( Prov. 6:16-19 ) ‘Would it interfere with my worship and perhaps keep me away from my family for long periods of time?’ If the answer to such questions is yes, it would be wise not to accept the job, even if work is hard to find. Because we walk by faith, we make decisions that show our conviction that Jehovah will somehow care for our needs.​— Matt. 6:33; Heb. 13:5 . w25.03 21 ¶5-6 December 21-27

daily.scripture: [ Be ] kind to one another, tenderly compassionate, freely forgiving one another.
daily.comment: We should always try to see our Christian brothers and sisters as Jehovah sees them. We do so by focusing on their positive qualities and not on their imperfections, which will eventually disappear. We can resolve any differences between us in a spirit of love. Then the spiritual paradise will attract people who want to be treated in a similar way. May we be forever grateful for the paradise that Jehovah has created for us. Anyone who wants to be refreshed, content, calm, and safe must come into the spiritual paradise and never leave it! Beware, though, because Satan is trying his best to lure us away from it. ( 1 Pet. 5:8; Rev. 12:9 ) We must not allow him to succeed. Let us vigorously protect the beauty, purity, and peace of the spiritual paradise. w24.04 24-25 ¶18-19 December 21-27

Parents, you can instill in your children zeal for Jehovah’s worship. Teach your children by word and example that spiritual matters​—such as studying the Bible, attending meetings, and participating in the field ministry—​take priority over all other activities. Otherwise your children might conclude that being one of Jehovah’s Witnesses is nothing more than belonging to the “family religion.” As a result, they might put true worship in second place or even leave it entirely. Is someone who has stopped serving Jehovah beyond hope? No, because he can repent and resume true worship. To do so, he may need to swallow his pride and accept help from congregation elders. ( Jas. 5:14 ) No effort he makes is too great if it results in his being restored to Jehovah’s favor! w24.07 24-25 ¶18-19 December 21-27

How can you keep your courtship honorable? As your feelings grow, you will naturally feel more attracted to each other. What can help you to keep yourselves morally clean? Avoid immoral conversations, being alone together, and heavy drinking. ( Eph. 5:3 ) These things can arouse passion and weaken your resolve to do what is right. Why not regularly discuss together what measures you can take to keep your courtship honorable? ( Prov. 22:3 ) Some displays of affection may be appropriate as your relationship progresses. However, if your passions are aroused, you will likely find it hard to think objectively about the other person. ( Song of Sol. 1:2; 2:6 ) Displays of affection can also easily escalate and lead to misconduct. ( Prov. 6:27 ) Therefore, early in your relationship, discuss what limits you will set, in harmony with Bible principles.​— 1 Thess. 4:3-7 . w24.05 29 ¶10-11 December 21-27
